intro: San Francisco was a town of a few hundred people in 1848 and Golden Gate Park was bare dunes into the 1870s, so every tree here was planted on purpose, and 150 years counts as old. Seven of the eight are city Landmark Trees, designated one at a time by ordinance: a cork oak atop a stairway street, an Australian fig outside a hospital, two flowering ash at a library door, the Dolores Street palms, the Quesada Avenue palms, and a Cole Valley pohutukawa that flowers yellow instead of red. The eighth is the tree the city lights every Christmas.
meta_description: Every tree in San Francisco was planted on purpose. The city's Landmark Trees, plus the cypress it has lit as its Christmas tree since 1929.
question_answer: Nobody has dated most of San Francisco's remarkable trees, so the honest answer is a planting era rather than an age. The oldest here is Uncle John's Tree, the Monterey cypress on the lawn outside McLaren Lodge at the eastern end of Golden Gate Park, which the park's historians put at planted around 1880, so roughly 135 to 155 years old. It is named for John McLaren, the park's long-serving superintendent, who died in 1943, and it has been lit as the city's Christmas tree since 1929. Of the other six, only the yellow-flowered pohutukawa on Stanyan Street has a planting era on record, the late 1950s; the rest carry no documented planting date, and the city's Landmark Tree register does not record one. If you know a date, or have a photograph old enough to help, tell us.
question_meta: Uncle John's Tree, a Monterey cypress planted around 1880 outside McLaren Lodge, is the oldest tree on this San Francisco page. Where to find it.
question_context: San Francisco keeps a Landmark Tree register rather than an ancient-tree register, and the difference explains this page. Trees are designated one at a time under Article 16 of the Public Works Code, on grounds of size, rarity or the part they play in a street, and the list runs to roughly twenty-five trees citywide. Seven of the eight here come off it. What that register does not record is age, and neither does anything else within reach: not the 2005 Board of Supervisors resolution that landmarked the bay laurel outside the Customs House, not the city's own entry for the Dolores Street palms, not Mike Sullivan's Trees of San Francisco, which is the standard reference for this city. That leaves the dating to circumstance. The gold rush arrived in 1849, Golden Gate Park was sand dunes until the 1870s, and the Mission and Bernal Heights streets these trees stand on were laid out later still, so a tree of 150 years is an early one by local reckoning. If you can date any of the seven, that is the gap this page would most like closed.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in San Francisco?
faq.a: Uncle John's Tree, the Monterey cypress outside McLaren Lodge in Golden Gate Park, planted around 1880 according to the park's historians. Of the others, only the yellow pohutukawa on Stanyan Street has a planting era on record, the late 1950s.

faq.q: What is a San Francisco Landmark Tree?
faq.a: A tree given individual protection by the city under Article 16 of the Public Works Code, designated one at a time and numbered. There are roughly twenty-five citywide, and six of them are on this page.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Six stand on public ground: a park lawn, two sidewalks, a street median, a library entrance and a public stairway garden. The yellow pohutukawa on Stanyan Street grows in the front garden of a private house and is seen from the public sidewalk. No tickets and no gates.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Four of them, at a stretch. The cork oak, the Dolores Street palms, the Moreton Bay fig and the flowering ash at the Bernal Heights library form a chain of about three kilometres downhill across Dolores Heights, the Mission and Bernal Heights. Golden Gate Park and the Financial District are separate trips.

trees.name: Uncle John's Tree

location.address: McLaren Lodge, 501 Stanyan Street, Golden Gate Park

verified_sources: https://goldengatepark.substack.com/p/two-christmas-trees (Susan Freinkel, fetched directly: 'Uncle John's Tree... Monterey cypress... Outside McLaren Lodge... planted around 1880; described as one of the oldest in the park')

https://richmondsunsetnews.com/2021/12/02/press-release-tree-lighting-ceremony-in-golden-gate-park-dec-2-2021/ (republished San Francisco Recreation and Park Department press release, fetched directly: 'Known as Uncle John's Tree in honor of Golden Gate Park's designer and first park superintendent John McLaren, the giant cypress was first illuminated with 800 bulbs on McLaren's 84th birthday'; caption confirms location 'at McLaren Lodge in Golden Gate Park')
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McLaren_Lodge (coordinates for McLaren Lodge building, fetched directly)
trees.access: Free, always open. Stands on the public lawn immediately outside McLaren Lodge, the SF Recreation and Parks headquarters building at the east end of Golden Gate Park.
trees.transport: MUNI bus lines on Fell/Oak or the N-Judah/5-Fulton corridor stop within a few minutes' walk; the tree stands right at the Panhandle entrance to the park.
trees.story:
San Francisco's Christmas tree has roots. The Monterey cypress on the lawn outside McLaren Lodge was first strung with 800 bulbs in 1929, on the birthday of John McLaren, the park superintendent the lodge is named for, and it has been lit almost every December since. McLaren asked on his deathbed that the lighting go on. He died in 1943, and it has.

The tree took his name too. Park historians put its planting at around 1880, which makes it roughly 135 to 155 years old and one of the oldest things growing in a park that was bare sand dunes when the city started work on it in the 1870s. Monterey cypress grows wild on a couple of headlands of the California coast and nowhere else on earth, which means a large one in a city park is a planted tree by definition rather than a survivor of anything.

No girth or height has been published for it, and no register carries a coordinate for the trunk, so the pin here marks McLaren Lodge, the parks department's own headquarters building at the Stanyan Street corner of the park. Walk to the front entrance and the cypress is the big one on the lawn.
trees.how_to_recognise: The large cypress on the open lawn directly in front of the McLaren Lodge entrance, at the Stanyan Street end of the park. In December it is the one carrying the lights.

trees.name: The Landmark Palms of Dolores Street

location.address: Dolores Street median at 730 Dolores Street (between 19th and Liberty Streets)

verified_sources: https://www.sfenvironment.org/landmark-tree-program (San Francisco Department of the Environment, official Landmark Tree list, fetched directly: lists 'Canary Island date palms (Phoenix canariensis), 730 Dolores Street median' and 'Cliff date palms (Phoenix rupicola), 730 Dolores Street median' as two of the city's officially designated Landmark Trees under Article 16 of the Public Works Code)

https://sfstandard.com/2023/01/18/could-sfs-iconic-palm-trees-disappear/ (The San Francisco Standard, fetched directly: 'Those beautiful palms lining Dolores Street? They are Canary Island date palms, beloved enough for the city to officially designate them as trees with landmark status.')
trees.access: Free, always visible from the sidewalk on either side of Dolores Street; the trees stand in the raised median that runs down the centre of the street, so they are seen rather than walked among.
trees.transport: J-Church Muni Metro runs the length of Dolores Street; the 33 and 24 bus lines cross it nearby. Street parking and a wide sidewalk on both sides.
trees.story:
The city's landmark list names this one block of Dolores Street twice. Once for the Canary Island date palms in the median, and once for a pair of cliff date palms, Phoenix rupicola, a rarer and finer-leaved cousin standing in the same strip of grass. Two designations, one address: 730 Dolores, the median between 19th and Liberty.

That is why this entry is a block rather than an avenue. Palms run down the middle of Dolores Street for most of its length, and a row of trunks a mile long is a view rather than somewhere to stand; the city itself picked out this stretch, and the two rare palms in it are the likeliest reason. The San Francisco Standard, writing in 2023 about whether the city's palms have a future, called them beloved, which for a street tree is a measurement of something.

Nobody we could reach has dated them. Canary Island date palms grow slowly and take decades to reach this height, and Dolores Street was rebuilt after the 1906 earthquake, but no source we read joins those two facts to these particular trunks, so this page leaves the age empty. If you have a planting record, or a photograph of this median without palms in it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: The raised median between 19th and Liberty. Most of the trunks are Canary Island date palms, heavy and thick; the two cliff date palms among them are slimmer, with finer, more drooping leaves.

trees.name: The Flowering Ash of Bernal Heights Library
verified_sources: https://www.sfenvironment.org/landmark-tree-program (San Francisco Department of the Environment, official Landmark Tree list, fetched directly: 'Flowering ash (Fraxinus ornus), 500 Cortland Street (Bernal Heights Library)')

http://www.sftrees.com/blog/2023/1/30/bernal-heights-south-tree-tour (Mike Sullivan, author of 'The Trees of San Francisco', fetched directly: '1. 500 Cortland ... Flowering ash trees (Fraxinus ornus), Spain to Austria, Lebanon, & Armenia (2 trees flanking the main entry to the library; official SF city landmark trees)')
trees.access: Free, always visible; the pair stands right at the main entrance of the Bernal Heights Branch Library, a public building open during library hours, on the public sidewalk edge regardless.
trees.transport: On Cortland Avenue, Bernal Heights' main commercial street; the 24-Divisadero and 67-Bernal Heights Muni bus lines run along or near Cortland.
trees.story:
Somebody chose well for a branch library door. Two flowering ash stand either side of the entrance at 500 Cortland Avenue, and the pair is on San Francisco's Landmark Tree list, which runs to only about twenty-five trees in the whole city. One of those designations went to the doorway of a neighbourhood branch library in Bernal Heights.

Fraxinus ornus is a southern European and Near Eastern tree, growing wild from Spain through Austria to Lebanon and Armenia, and it is an odd thing to find flanking a civic building in California. It is small, it is neat, and it earns its common name once a year when the whole crown goes over to creamy plumes of flower. Mike Sullivan, who wrote the book on this city's trees, has the pair on his own Bernal Heights walking tour, one stop, both trees.

That is how to treat it. You stand at the library door and you have seen the entry; there is nothing to hunt for. No planting date exists for either tree in the city's file or in Sullivan's, so their age is anybody's guess, and a librarian or a neighbour who remembers them going in would settle it in a sentence. Cortland Avenue is the main street of the neighbourhood, so the walk up is worth having anyway.
trees.how_to_recognise: Two small ash trees, one on each side of the main entrance to the Bernal Heights Branch Library at 500 Cortland Avenue. Both trees together are the entry.

best_time.label: April and May, when the crowns fill with creamy flower plumes and the name makes sense

trees.name: The Cork Oak of 20th Street

location.address: Public right-of-way stairway garden on 20th Street at Noe Street (top of the Cork Oak Tree Community Garden)

verified_sources: https://www.sfenvironment.org/landmark-tree-program (San Francisco Department of the Environment, official Landmark Tree list, fetched directly: 'Cork Oak (Quercus suber), Public right-of-way on 20th Street at Noe Street')

https://doloresheights.org/2025/10/13/cork-oak-tree-garden-at-20th-noe-streets/ (Dolores Heights Improvement Club, neighbourhood association, fetched directly: 'The hillside garden at 20th and Noe Streets is renamed the "Cork Oak Tree Community Garden" in recognition and celebration of its official San Francisco Landmark Tree No. 15 (Quercus suber), at the top of the garden.')
https://doloresheights.org/2025/10/13/cork-oak-tree-garden-at-20th-noe-streets/
trees.access: Free, always open. Stands at the top of a public hillside stairway garden in the street's own public right-of-way, tended by the neighbourhood association with city (SFDPW) support; not on private land at any point.
trees.transport: In the Castro/Noe Valley/Dolores Heights hillside; the 24-Divisadero and 33-Ashbury/18th bus lines pass nearby, and it is a walkable hill climb from either Church Street or Castro Street Muni stops.
trees.story:
San Francisco Landmark Tree No. 15 grows in the middle of a street. Not beside one: 20th Street at Noe is one of this city's stairway streets, a public right-of-way that was never paved as a roadway, and the hillside garden climbing it stands where the road would have gone. The cork oak stands at the top of it, on ground that legally belongs to the street.

In October 2025 the neighbourhood association that tends the garden renamed the whole thing after the tree, so it is now the Cork Oak Tree Community Garden. They keep it watered with help from the city's public works and water departments, which is an unusually specific piece of care for a tree nobody owns.

Quercus suber is the tree the cork industry is built on, a Mediterranean oak grown in Portugal and Spain for a bark thick enough to be stripped every nine years or so and grow back. Nobody harvests this one. It is evergreen, so there is no season to wait for, and no source we found gives a planting date or a girth, which leaves the age open; if you know when it went in, that is worth a message. The climb up from Noe Street is the price of admission.
trees.how_to_recognise: At the top of the stepped hillside garden on 20th Street at Noe, not at the bottom. The bark is deeply corky and spongy to the touch, unlike anything else planted on the block.

official_register.name: San Francisco Landmark Tree (Public Works Code Article 16), no. 15

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of St. Luke's

location.address: Valencia Street, south of Cesar Chavez Street, west side, near CPMC Mission Bernal (formerly St. Luke's Hospital), 3555 Cesar Chavez Street

verified_sources: https://www.sfenvironment.org/landmark-tree-program (San Francisco Department of the Environment, official Landmark Tree list, fetched directly: 'Moreton Bay fig (Ficus macrophylla), 3555 Cesar Chavez Street')

http://www.sftrees.com/landmark-trees (Mike Sullivan, author of 'The Trees of San Francisco', fetched directly: 'Ficus macrophylla (Moreton Bay Fig): Valencia Street south of Cesar Chavez, west side of street near St. Luke's Hospital (very large specimen)')

https://burritojustice.com/2009/07/31/know-your-trees/ (fetched directly, corroborating: 'the huge Moreton Bay fig in front of St. Luke's on Valencia', described as protected/landmarked, with a photo of 'our Valencia Street moreton bay fig in all its glory')
trees.access: Free, always visible from the public sidewalk on Valencia Street; stands on hospital grounds fronting the street rather than inside a fenced garden.
trees.transport: On Valencia Street at Cesar Chavez, in the Mission/Bernal Heights border; the 14, 49 and 67 Muni bus lines all pass within a couple of blocks.
trees.story:
Los Angeles, Santa Barbara and San Diego have the grand Moreton Bay figs. San Francisco has this one, and the species is genuinely uncommon this far up the coast, where the summers are cool and the fog comes in for days at a time. It is an Australian rainforest tree, a banyan relative whose big specimens spread a wide crown over roots that buttress out along the ground, and Mike Sullivan, who wrote the standard book on this city's trees, files it simply as a very large specimen.

The city's Landmark Tree list carries it, and a local history blog photographed it in 2009 and noted it had lately lost a branch, which is what happens to a crown this heavy on a street corner.

The address is the thing to know before you go. The city register files it under 3555 Cesar Chavez Street, the hospital it stands in front of, and you will not find the tree on Cesar Chavez. It is around the corner on Valencia Street, west side, just south of the junction, fronting the grounds rather than fenced inside them, so the sidewalk is close enough. Nobody has published an age or a girth for it, which for a fig of this size is a gap worth closing.
trees.how_to_recognise: On Valencia Street rather than on Cesar Chavez: west side, just south of the junction, in front of the hospital. It is the wide-crowned evergreen fig, far bigger than anything else on the block.

trees.name: The Sweet Bay at the Customs House

location.address: 555 Battery Street, northwest corner of Battery and Jackson Streets (United States Customs House)

verified_sources: https://www.sfenvironment.org/landmark-tree-program (San Francisco Department of the Environment, official Landmark Tree list, fetched directly: 'Sweet bay (Laurus nobilis), 555 Battery Street')

http://www.sftrees.com/landmark-trees (Mike Sullivan, author of 'The Trees of San Francisco', fetched directly: 'Laurus nobilis (sweet bay, Grecian laurel): 555 Battery/Jackson (NW corner Washington/Battery) in the Financial District')

https://sfbos.org/ftp/uploadedfiles/bdsupvrs/resolutions05/r0670-05.pdf (San Francisco Board of Supervisors Resolution No. 670-05, the formal 2005 landmark designation; found via search and the PDF was fetched but its text is encoded with a non-standard font mapping that could not be extracted cleanly with the tools available this pass, so it is listed as evidence of the resolution's existence but not quoted from)
trees.access: Free, always visible. Stands on the public sidewalk at the corner of the United States Customs House, a federal government building; the tree itself is on the public right-of-way.
trees.transport: Financial District / Jackson Square, a short walk from the Embarcadero BART/Muni station and several Financial District bus lines.
trees.story:
The tree the Romans cut their victory crowns from is growing on a Financial District sidewalk, outside a federal customs house. Sweet bay, bay laurel, Grecian laurel: one Mediterranean species, Laurus nobilis, the laurel of laureates and of the leaves in a pot of stock, standing at the northwest corner of Battery and Jackson.

San Francisco landmarked it formally. The Board of Supervisors passed resolution 670-05 in 2005, which is the kind of paperwork usually spent on buildings, and Mike Sullivan's Trees of San Francisco pins it to the same corner, in front of the United States Customs House. The tree is on the public right-of-way, so the federal building behind it changes nothing about walking up.

It is a sensible tree for this city, whatever the classical associations. Laurus nobilis comes from a climate of dry summers and wet winters, which is San Francisco's own, and it takes wind and fog without complaint, both of which the corner supplies. No age, girth or height has been published for it anywhere we could reach, so how long it has stood on this corner is an open question, and one a reader with the right city record could close in a sentence. Jackson Square around it is a good walk regardless.
trees.how_to_recognise: The evergreen on the northwest corner of Battery and Jackson, in front of the Customs House. Crush a leaf: it is the bay leaf out of the kitchen cupboard.

trees.name: The Yellow Christmas Tree of Stanyan Street

location.address: 1221 Stanyan Street, in front of the house

verified_sources: https://sfpublicworks.org/services/significant-and-landmark-trees (SF Public Works official list of designated Landmark Trees: '1221 Stanyan Street: New Zealand Christmas Tree')

http://www.sftrees.com/blog/2016/5/30/my-favorite-tree (Mike Sullivan, 2016: yellow mutation from Motiti Island 1940, cutting planted in front of 1221 Stanyan by Victor Reiter's family, 'more than 70 years later thriving', blooms yellow around Memorial Day, seen from the street)
https://www.sfenvironment.org/landmark-tree-program (seen only via search result; page 403s to fetchers; designation by Urban Forestry Council 2019, unanimous vote)
trees.access: Visible from the public sidewalk on Stanyan Street; it stands in front of a private home, so look from the pavement only.
trees.transport: Muni N Judah or 6/7 to Haight St and Stanyan, short walk (stop not verified)
trees.story:
The pohutukawa, the New Zealand Christmas tree, flowers red. This one flowers yellow. The yellow form began as a natural mutation, found on Motiti Island in New Zealand's Bay of Plenty in 1940, in a species that otherwise blooms crimson.

Victor Reiter got hold of a cutting in the late 1950s and his family planted it in front of their home at 1221 Stanyan Street, on the edge of Cole Valley. The local tree writer Mike Sullivan, writing in 2016, called it his favourite tree in the city and found it thriving more than seventy years after that first yellow plant turned up. In 2019 the Urban Forestry Council voted unanimously to make it an official Landmark Tree.

Its moment comes around Memorial Day, at the end of May, when it blooms, and the flowers can still cover it in late June. Every other New Zealand Christmas tree you pass in the city flowers red.

This is a front garden, not a park, and the right way to see it is from the public pavement on Stanyan Street, without stepping off it. Our pin marks the address rather than the trunk.

The city still lists it among its landmark trees, but the newest dated photograph we have found is from June 2012, when it was in full yellow flower. Nobody has published its girth. If you photograph it from the pavement in flower, send it to us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in early summer by its yellow flowers, where the city's other New Zealand Christmas trees bloom red. It stands in front of the house at 1221 Stanyan Street; look from the pavement.

best_time.label: late May into June, when it blooms yellow instead of red

trees.name: The Canary Palms of Quesada Avenue

location.address: Quesada Avenue median, just west of 3rd Street

verified_sources: https://sfpublicworks.org/services/significant-and-landmark-trees (SF Public Works official list: 'Quesada Street Median (West of 3rd Street to dead end): 13 Canary Island Date Palms')
https://www.sanfranciscostory.com/quesada-gardens/ (fetched directly: median planted around 1920 with Canary Island Date Palms, same as Dolores Street; palms survived the twentieth century)
trees.access: Free, public street median in the Bayview; walk along the sidewalk.
trees.transport: Muni T Third or the 15 bus on 3rd Street, then a short walk west on Quesada (stop not verified)
trees.verify_notes: Official Landmark Tree group of 13 palms on one compact block, one place to stand (like the Dolores palms already published as sfo_002). Planting date conflict: sanfranciscostory.com says about 1920; a search summary (lead only) says about 1932. Do not narrow. Pin: Nominatim places Quesada Avenue between roughly 37.7299,-122.3854 and 37.7331,-122.3911; I set an approximate mid-block point, NOT checked on aerial imagery. lifecheck NONE at pin: alive evidence is only the official list and undated-recent articles; flag. Girth and height unknown.
trees.story:
Thirteen Canary Island date palms line the median of Quesada Avenue in the Bayview, and San Francisco counts all thirteen as one Landmark Tree. Public Works lists them that way: the Quesada Street median, from just west of 3rd Street to the dead end, 13 palms.

They are the same species as the far better known palms down the middle of Dolores Street. Local history has the Quesada median planted with them around 1920. One account puts it closer to 1932, and we have not been able to settle which, so call them roughly a century old, give or take a decade.

What they have seen since is most of the Bayview's twentieth century, and they outlasted all of it; the city's current landmark list still carries all thirteen. A palm of this kind holds no rings to count, and nobody has published the height or the girth of any of the thirteen, so the age rests on the planting date alone.

This is a street, not a park, and that is the appeal: the whole landmark stands on one compact block, so there is one place to go and thirteen trees to count. Walk the sidewalk rather than the median itself.

Our pin is a mid-block point that has not been checked against aerial imagery, so treat it as the street rather than a spot. The 3rd Street end is the easy one to find. If you know when these palms were really planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the row of thirteen Canary Island date palms down the median of Quesada Avenue, running west from 3rd Street to the dead end.
